newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China TCK wheat ban seen based on scientific study.
newsitem.headline: China TCK wheat ban seen based on scientific study.

text.p: China's refusal to import U.S. wheat tainted with an untreatable fungus that can dramatically slash crop yields is justified on scientific grounds, agricultural experts said on Tuesday.

The Asia Pacific Plant Protection Commission plans to list TCK smut as a quarantine pest in the region because it can cut wheat yields by up to 30 percent, said Wendy Ko, agricultural officer with the Hong Kong Agriculture and Fisheries Department.
"TCK is not a political issue," Ko said in an interview.
"Individual countries should have the right to protect their own economies. China doesn't have this problem and so doesn't want this problem," Ko said.
The fungus cannibalises the wheat, she said, with the black spores replacing the grain embryos within the husk. It also stunts the plant's growth.
Fungicides were useless againt TCK spores, Ko said, as they have a highly resistant coat. The spores can spread rapidly on wind and pass intact through the digestive systems of grazing animals.

Beijing is within its rights to refuse to accept the import of any agricultural products feared to carry dangerous pests, a senior technical officer with the commission, P.K. Saha, said by telephone from Bangkok.
"It is an issue between the two parties," Saha said, adding: "China is well within its rights to refuse to accept wheat from the United States on technical grounds."
TCK smut has been a simmering bilateral issue between Washington and Beijing since 1974, when China declared zero tolerance for imports of wheat tainted with the fungus.

The United States has also pointed to Canada, which sells around five million tonnes of wheat a year to China. The Canadian Wheat Board says its product is free of TCK, though Ko says, as does Washington, the fungus has been found there, too.
China is one of the world's biggest wheat importing nations and is the United States' biggest wheat customer.

Since 1991, according to figures from Washington's wheat marketing arm U.S. Wheat Associates, China's purchases of U.S. wheat have averaged $600 million a year. The value of imports peaked at $1.1 billion in 1988/89.
In the marketing year ended July 31, China bought 3.8 million tonnes of U.S. wheat worth $700 million.
But a new get-tough approach by Beijing has seen China this year reject contaminated wheat and warn international trading firms it is their responsibility not to ship tainted grain.
China is not likely to need to import U.S. wheat for the remainder of 1996 as a bumper crop has just been harvested and Canada and Australia can pick up any slack in supply.
But trading sources have said that China will eventually need to go back to the United States and the two sides must come up with a face-saving way out of the current impasse.
